title: Chapter 3 Mastery Quiz: Variables, Measurement & Psychometrics
description: Test your mastery of independent/dependent variables, NOIR scales, reliability types, and construct validity dimensions.

questions.question: In an experiment testing whether chewing gum improves exam performance, what is the Independent Variable (IV)?

options.text: Chewing gum condition (gum vs. no gum)

questions.explanation: The variable manipulated by the experimenter (presence or absence of chewing gum) is the Independent Variable.

questions.question: What is the defining characteristic of a confounding variable?

options.text: It varies randomly across all conditions without systematic pattern
It systematically co-varies with the independent variable, offering an alternative explanation for changes in the dependent variable
It is always measured on a nominal scale
It can be removed by increasing the alpha level

questions.explanation: A confounding variable varies systematically along with the independent variable, making it impossible to isolate the true causal agent.

questions.question: Which of the following variables is measured on a Nominal scale?

options.text: Psychiatric diagnosis (e.g., Bipolar I, Major Depression, Schizophrenia)

questions.explanation: Psychiatric diagnoses are qualitative category labels without numerical or hierarchical ranking, representing a nominal scale.

questions.question: Why is the finishing order of runners in a 100-meter dash (1st, 2nd, 3rd) considered an Ordinal scale rather than an Interval scale?

options.text: Because runners do not wear numbers
The differences in elapsed time between 1st and 2nd may be 0.02s, while between 2nd and 3rd may be 0.85s (intervals are unequal)
Because ordinal scales have a true zero point
Because ordinal scales only apply to animals

questions.explanation: Ordinal scales reflect rank order, but the spacing or difference between consecutive ranks is typically unequal and unstandardized.

questions.question: What is the crucial mathematical feature that distinguishes a Ratio scale from an Interval scale?

options.text: An absolute, non-arbitrary true zero point
The ability to calculate the mode

questions.explanation: A ratio scale possesses an absolute true zero point where zero signifies total absence of the variable, allowing valid ratio statements (e.g., twice as much).

questions.question: Why is Temperature in degrees Celsius considered an Interval scale rather than a Ratio scale?

options.text: Because it cannot be measured indoors
Zero degrees Celsius is an arbitrary freezing point, not the total absence of molecular thermal energy
Because European and American thermometers use different mercury
Because interval scales do not permit subtraction

questions.explanation: Zero degrees Celsius does not represent absolute zero heat energy (0 Kelvin does); therefore, 20°C is not 'twice as warm' as 10°C.

questions.question: What does psychometric reliability measure?

options.text: Whether a test measures the theoretical construct it intends to measure
The consistency and repeatability of a measurement procedure
Whether the study passes an IRB review

questions.explanation: Reliability reflects the precision, stability, and reproducibility of a measurement instrument across repeated administrations.

questions.question: Administering a personality inventory to 100 participants today and readministering the exact same inventory 4 weeks later evaluates which type of reliability?
questions.explanation: Administering the same test to the same sample at two different time points directly evaluates Test-Retest Reliability.

questions.question: Two independent clinical psychologists watch video recordings of 50 patient interviews and code each patient for signs of clinical depression. What reliability metric evaluates their agreement?
questions.explanation: Inter-rater reliability measures the degree of consistency or agreement between two or more independent raters or observers.

questions.question: Which statistical index is most commonly reported to document the internal consistency of a multi-item psychological questionnaire?
questions.explanation: Cronbach's alpha is the standard psychometric metric assessing the degree to which all items on a scale measure the same underlying construct.

questions.question: What is generally accepted as the minimum threshold for satisfactory internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) in psychological research?
questions.explanation: In psychology, a Cronbach's alpha of 0.70 or higher is widely considered acceptable for research purposes (0.80+ for clinical screening).

questions.question: Can a psychological test be valid if it is completely unreliable?

options.text: Yes, validity and reliability are completely independent
No, reliability is a necessary prerequisite for validity
Yes, but only if approved by an IRB
Only if the sample size exceeds 1,000 participants

questions.explanation: If a test produces erratic, noisy scores with high measurement error, it cannot consistently capture the true construct; reliability is required for validity.

questions.question: A panel of expert neuropsychologists reviews an attention-deficit diagnostic test to confirm that it samples all clinical dimensions of ADHD (inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity). What type of validity is being evaluated?
questions.explanation: Content validity evaluates whether a test comprehensively covers all relevant components and facets of the intended conceptual construct.

questions.question: Which of the following describes Face Validity?

options.text: Whether a test looks plausible and relevant on its surface to a casual test-taker
The mathematical correlation between two parallel test forms
The statistical power of a repeated measures ANOVA

questions.explanation: Face validity refers to the subjective, superficial appearance that an assessment seems relevant to what it intends to measure.

questions.question: Demonstrating that SAT scores correlate significantly with first-year university GPA provides evidence for which form of validity?
questions.explanation: Predictive criterion validity occurs when test scores successfully predict a future concrete behavioral or academic outcome.

questions.question: A newly designed 10-item anxiety inventory correlates strongly (r = 0.81) with an established gold-standard anxiety questionnaire administered at the exact same session. This demonstrates:
questions.explanation: Concurrent validity evaluates how well a new measurement correlates with an established criterion or validated measure assessed simultaneously.

questions.question: What is Convergent Validity?

options.text: The degree to which an operational measure correlates strongly with measures of theoretically related constructs
The correlation between two completely unrelated concepts like height and empathy
The speed of mathematical calculation on computers
The agreement between an IRB and IACUC committee

questions.explanation: Convergent validity is shown when empirical measures of constructs that should theoretically be related actually show strong correlations.

questions.question: A researcher shows that a measure of 'Self-Compassion' correlates near zero (r = -0.04) with 'Grammatical Spelling Ability'. This finding is evidence of:
questions.explanation: Discriminant validity confirms that an instrument does not correlate with measures of conceptually distinct, unrelated traits.

questions.question: Which of the following is considered a 'Participant/Subject Variable' that cannot be randomly assigned in an experiment?

options.text: Font color of flashcards (blue vs. red)

questions.explanation: Chronological age is an intrinsic biological characteristic of the participant that cannot be manipulated or randomly assigned by the experimenter.

questions.question: What happens when an extraneous variable varies randomly rather than systematically across experimental conditions?

options.text: It becomes a confounding variable that invalidates causal conclusions
It adds random error variance (noise), slightly lowering statistical power, but does not bias the direction of results
It automatically converts the study into a meta-analysis
It forces the researcher to use a nominal measurement scale

questions.explanation: Randomly varying extraneous variables create unsystematic noise that may obscure subtle effects, but they do not systematically bias results or confound the IV.

questions.question: Under Classical Test Theory, what does an individual's Observed Score represent?

options.text: True Score multiplied by sample size

questions.explanation: Classical Test Theory models every observed score as the sum of a hypothetical true score plus random measurement error (X = T + E).

questions.question: Which of the following measurements represents an Interval scale?

options.text: Standard score on the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS IQ)
Number of siblings a child has

questions.explanation: Standardized IQ scores have equal numeric intervals (15 points per standard deviation) but lack a true zero point (score of 0 does not mean zero intelligence).
